name: Graciano

lines.s10: Graciano is Rioja's seasoning grape: a little of it brings deep colour, sharp freshness and a scent of violet to the blend.
lines.s20: Graciano is an old red of Rioja, used in small shares to give a blend colour, acidity and perfume. Alone it is deep purple and lively, with blackberry, violet and a cool touch of mint.
lines.s45: Graciano is used like salt in Rioja: a little lifts the whole blend. A native of Rioja, grown there and in Navarra, it ripens late and bears small crops. In the glass it is deep purple, with blackberry, black cherry and violet. The acidity is sharp, with a cool note of mint and a firm grip. Blenders add a few per cent to the long aged Riojas for colour and freshness, and a few cellars bottle it alone. Pour it with lamb chops, venison or a hard sheep's cheese. Growers once pulled it out for easier vines, and it nearly vanished before Rioja brought it back.
lines.sale: Graciano is the grape many Rioja lovers have tasted without knowing it, here on its own: violet, blackberry and a fresh, firm bite. Open it with the lamb chops for a table that wants something new from a region it already trusts.

glass.lead: Blackberry, black cherry and violet in a deep purple glass, with liquorice, a cool note of mint and sharp, fresh acidity.

ladder.where: Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, on warmer, sheltered plots
Rioja Oriental, Navarra and South Australia

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin medium plus to high, alcohol medium to medium plus, body medium plus, and deep in colour.

home.home: Rioja, with Navarra beside it, where it ripens late and yields little. A few per cent in a Reserva or Gran Reserva brings colour, acidity and violet that help the wine keep for decades. It nearly vanished as growers chose easier vines, and its revival now gives a few varietal bottlings too.
home.abroad: Portugal knows it as Tinta Miúda, a minor grape of Lisboa, Corsica as Minustellu and Sardinia as Cagnulari. Australia grows a little, mostly in South Australia, as a deep coloured varietal or with Tempranillo.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, as for Rioja and other medium reds.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl.
service.decant: Consider it for a young varietal Graciano after tasting a sample; it can be tight and firm.
service.age: Varietal wines open over five to ten years; its acidity helps a Gran Reserva blend keep for decades.

with.why: sharp acidity and grip cut the fat
blackberry and firm tannin suit lean, dark meat
fresh acidity lifts a rich, slow cooked sauce
salt and fat soften the firm grip

labels.means: A two grape blend named on the label: Tempranillo leads, Graciano adds colour and lift.
Graciano's Portuguese name, a minor grape in the reds of Lisboa.
Graciano's name in Sardinia, mostly in the north west of the island.
Graciano's Corsican name, one of the old island grapes rescued in recent decades.

guest.q: I have never heard of Graciano. What is it?
guest.a: A native red of Rioja that growers almost lost because it bears such small crops. A few per cent in a Rioja blend adds colour, freshness and a scent of violet, and a few cellars bottle it alone.

guest.q: Why is there so little of it?
guest.a: It ripens late and yields little, so growers pulled it out for easier vines. Rioja and Navarra have replanted it, but it is still a small share of most blends.

guest.q: Will a young varietal Graciano be too firm tonight?
guest.a: It is fresh and firm when young. With a fatty cut of lamb and a little air it softens, and I can pour you a taste first.

compare.tell: Tempranillo is rounder and softer in acidity, with strawberry and leather; Graciano is deeper in colour and sharper, with violet, mint and liquorice.
Carignan, Mazuelo in Rioja, shares the acidity and tannin but brings cranberry, dried thyme and an iron note; Graciano is more perfumed, with violet and mint.
Mourvèdre is gamey and meaty, with leather on a fuller, warmer frame; Graciano is fresher and more perfumed, with violet and mint.

profile.st: Deep purple, nearly opaque · Body medium plus · Acid high · Tannin medium plus to high · Alcohol medium to medium plus · Dry
profile.fruit: Blackberry, black cherry and mulberry; red cherry and raspberry from cooler sites
profile.other: Violet, liquorice, black pepper and clove, with a cool lift of mint
profile.tell: Deep colour and sharp acidity with violet and mint: the perfume and bite a little Graciano gives a Rioja blend
profile.regions: Rioja and Navarra; Lisboa as Tinta Miúda, Corsica as Minustellu, Sardinia as Cagnulari; a little in South Australia
profile.confuse: Tempranillo is softer and rounder, with strawberry and leather; Carignan is as sharp but brings cranberry, dried thyme and iron, not violet

cards.front: Graciano: what does a few per cent of it add to a Rioja blend?
cards.back: Deep colour, fresh acidity and a scent of violet, which help Reserva and Gran Reserva wines keep for many years.

cards.front: Why did Graciano nearly disappear from Rioja's vineyards?
cards.back: It ripens late and yields little, so growers replaced it with easier vines. A revival has brought it back, in blends and in a few varietal wines.

cards.front: Graciano travels under other names. Which in Portugal, Corsica and Sardinia?
cards.back: Tinta Miúda in Portugal, chiefly in Lisboa; Minustellu in Corsica; Cagnulari in Sardinia.

questions.q: A varietal red from Rioja is poured blind: deep purple, with blackberry, violet, mint and liquorice, sharp acidity and a firm grip. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour, sharp acidity, violet and mint mark Graciano. Mazuelo, Rioja's Carignan and the nearest miss, is as firm but brings cranberry, dried thyme and an iron note, not violet.

questions.q: A guest reading a Portuguese list asks which grape in an Alenquer red is the same as Rioja's Graciano. Which name do you point to?
questions.exp: Tinta Miúda is Graciano under its Portuguese name, a minor grape of Lisboa. Tinta Roriz, the nearest miss, is a Rioja grape too, but it is Tempranillo.

questions.q: A guest reading the back label of a Rioja Gran Reserva asks why its small share of Graciano was nearly lost from the vineyards. What do you tell him?
opts: It ripens late and bears small crops
The law long banned it from Rioja
It ripens too early for the valley
It cannot take long ageing in oak
questions.exp: Graciano ripens late and yields little, so growers replaced it with easier vines until a revival. Ripening early, the nearest wrong answer, is Tempranillo's trait and gave it its name.

report: A new grape, mode home as the plan fixes it. No TASTE row exists, so nothing can contradict TASTE.world.

Late ripening, low yield, high acidity, deep colour and its role in Reserva and Gran Reserva blends, its near disappearance and violet stand on the Codex's own Rioja and Navarra records and its Régionale question i-p8jvlek9, and on the Rioja consejo's two pages (late ripening and low fertility; acidity higher than the other Rioja grapes; intense colour, rich tannin; red and black fruit, liquorice, flowers, cherries, pepper and a hint of mint). Tinta Miúda and Minustellu stand on the Codex's Lisboa and Corsica records; Cagnulari in Sardinia on the Wein-Plus glossary and Wine Grapes.

Australia, mostly South Australia, stands on Wine Australia's alternative varieties guide as search quoted it and on trade reviews of Langhorne Creek and Padthaway wines that name producers and so are not cited. California and Texas plantings were seen in one trade page each and are left out.

The floral group carries violet and dried violet, and the herbal group mint and menthol: violet and mint are what the sources give, and a second floral note was not found in two sources. The alcohol is written medium to medium plus for want of a source that fixes it; a checker may tighten it.

The name's origin could not be confirmed and is left out. The Codex's Régionale question i-cpt5lfrq on Monastrell offers Graciano, called Morrastel in France as a distractor; Morrastel names Graciano in parts of France and Monastrell in Spain, a muddle this entry leaves alone.
